nameStory: Striped squill gets its name from the delicate dark stripes that run down the center of each white petal, creating a charming pinstriped pattern. The word 'squill' comes from the Greek 'skilla,' originally referring to sea onions and other bulbous plants. It's also called Lebanon squill after one of its native homelands in the mountains of Western Asia.
description: Striped squill is a small, early-blooming bulb that stands just 4-6 inches tall when in flower. It produces clusters of tiny, bell-shaped white flowers with distinctive blue or purple stripes running down each petal. The narrow, grass-like leaves emerge alongside the flowers in early spring. This charming little plant is native to Western Asia and the Caucasus but has naturalized in some New England gardens and occasionally escapes cultivation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: 2-3 narrow, strap-like leaves that feel smooth and slightly succulent, emerging directly from the ground at the same time as flowers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant reaching only 4-6 inches tall, with flowers clustered in a short spike at the top of a single stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Sweet, honey-like fragrance that's most noticeable on warm, still days when you get close to the blooms

habitat: In New England, striped squill is primarily found in cultivated gardens, particularly rock gardens and naturalized woodland edges where it has escaped from cultivation. It prefers well-drained soil and partial shade, often appearing near old homesites or established perennial beds. You might spot it in areas with other early spring bulbs like crocuses and snowdrops.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear very early, often while snow still lingers, blooming from late March through April with their distinctive striped petals and sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Leaves gradually yellow and die back by early summer as the plant enters dormancy, leaving no visible trace above ground.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no above-ground growth visible, though the bulb is developing next year's flower buds underground.
seasonality.winter: No visible growth above ground, existing only as a small bulb beneath the soil surface.

funFact: Despite being only 4-6 inches tall, striped squill can live for decades in the same spot, slowly multiplying underground to form charming colonies that pop up like tiny soldiers each spring, sometimes outliving the gardens where they were originally planted!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small white spring bulbs like snowdrops or glory-of-the-snow, but the distinctive blue or purple pinstripes down each petal are unique to striped squill. Memory trick: think 'striped squill, striped petals' – no other early bulb has this pinstriped pattern.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is sometimes called Lebanon squill, but it's not related to the true squills (Scilla species) despite the similar name. The confusion comes from both having small bulbs and early spring flowers, but they belong to different plant groups within the asparagus family.
compareHints: Striped squill is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among early spring bulbs. Compared to similar plants in the asparagus family like grape hyacinth or true squills, striped squill is distinguished by its white petals with dark stripes rather than solid blue or purple flowers. Its bell-shaped flowers and sweet fragrance also set it apart from the more tubular or star-shaped flowers of its relatives.
